items.title: SGA-based volleyball teaching with explicit life skills instruction is associated with technical-tactical, psychosocial, and motivational improvements in school students
items.abstract: This quasi-experimental study examined whether a school volleyball unit based on the Step-Game-Approach model combined with explicit life skills teaching (SGA + LS) was associated with changes in technical-tactical performance, life skills, motivation, and perception of success. Eighty-eight students aged 10–12 years participated in a quasi-experimental repeated-measures design with three groups: SGA + LS, direct instruction, and control. The intervention comprised 18 Physical Education classes. Outcomes were assessed before and/or after the intervention using IAD-VB, Life Skills Scale for Sport, Behavioral Regulation in Sport Questionnaire, and Perception of Success Questionnaire. Generalized Estimating Equations tested group, time, and group×time effects. Significant group × time interactions that remained significant after false discovery rate correction were observed for goal setting, Wald χ²(2) = 11.875, pFDR=0.009, time management, Wald χ²(2) = 10.203, pFDR=0.014, and communication, Wald χ²(2) = 7.538, pFDR=0.044. All technical-tactical outcomes showed significant adjusted interactions, Wald χ²(2) = 10.764–60.676, pFDR≤0.012, with both volleyball-specific conditions showing improvements across several outcomes. At post-test, SGA + LS showed higher decision-making than control, whereas SGA + LS and direct instruction did not differ significantly after Holm adjustment. For motivational regulation, significant adjusted interactions remained for identified regulation, global intrinsic motivation, goal achievement, stimulating experiences, and knowledge mastery, pFDR≤0.021. No adjusted group × time effect was observed for perceptions of success. Overall, the findings indicate selective rather than uniform associations between SGA + LS and technical-tactical, psychosocial, and motivational outcomes in school Physical Education.

items.title: Smart Automation For Ergonomic Risk Management In Sustainable Garment Manufacturing: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Garment manufacturing is a labor-intensive industry characterized by routine activities and awkward postures with physical demands, which makes employees vulnerable to a series of ergonomic risks. These risks negatively impact worker health and productivity. Emerging technologies like smart automation and robotics provide relevant solutions to mitigate this, improving workplace safety and overall working conditions. However, there are limitations and gaps in existing literature on ergonomics risk mitigation in garment manufacturing. These pertain to common ergonomics risks, their factors and impact, ergonomics risk mitigation strategies, and technological solutions. To identify these gaps, this study conducted a systematic literature review of 102 peer-reviewed articles published from 2010 to 2025 by synthesizing ergonomic risk and its factors, their effects on workers, and technological and strategic mitigation approaches. To ensure a focused review, four inclusion criteria were applied: (1) papers published between 2010 and 2025, (2) alignment with disciplines like Engineering, (3) inclusion of only research articles, (4) English-language articles. The review revealed that common ergonomic risks in garment manufacturing such as repetitive motion, awkward postures, and prolonged static positions, are major contributors to musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). Furthermore, the ergonomic risk factors were physical, environmental, and organizational. Moreover, these risks have a significant effect on workers' health and overall operational efficiency. Consequently, smart automation technologies like robotic systems, wearable exoskeletons, and ergonomically designed workstations emerge as relevant interventions for those risks. This study’s findings provide evidence-based insights to improve workers' health and productivity, and future directions and implications for managers, policymakers, and practitioners in garment manufacturing. Keywords: Ergonomics, Garment Manufacturing Industry, Innovation, Risk Management, Smart Automation, and Sustainable development

items.title: Students’ conceptions of artificial intelligence and machine learning in K–12 education: a systematic review
items.abstract: Background and context Knowing students’ conceptions of computer science phenomena is essential for the design of teaching–learning settings and instruments. They are particularly interesting in teaching artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) concepts. Therefore, a comprehensive synthesis focused on K–12 is essential to provide educators with actionable conceptions for curriculum design and assessment.Objective We investigate common conceptions of AI/ML in K–12 and to which curricular concepts these can be assigned. We also examine how conceptions vary across age/grade groups and the data collection/evaluation methods employed. This study uniquely synthesizes fragmented research on students’ conceptions of AI/ML into a unified snapshot, offering a systematic mapping that informs curriculum recommendations.Method A systematic literature review according to PRISMA is used to identify the relevant studies. We analyzed the selected literature, extracted the student conceptions, and classified them according to the curricular concepts.Findings We identified 27 relevant studies (from 2007 to 2024) including the conceptions of 1,077 K–12 students from 30 different countries. In addition, our data includes further information on the type of school, age/grade levels, genders and nationalities, the availability of the collected data, and the survey and evaluation methods used. We took a closer look at 29 of the 409 resulting, highly prevalent conceptions, which stand out due to their frequent occurrence.Implications Our findings may be useful for determining in which grade levels interventions targeting specific concepts would be most effective. This could also be used to study the development of these conceptions or developing assessments.

items.title: Team cognition in remote maritime operations: a scoping review and cross-domain theoretical synthesis
items.abstract: Introduction Remote maritime operations increasingly depend on complex, distributed socio-technical systems in which safe and effective performance relies on team cognition rather than on individual decision-making alone. Despite its importance, the conceptualisation and measurement of team cognition in this domain remain fragmented and underdeveloped. Methods A scoping review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Searches of SCOPUS, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost yielded 162 records, of which 51 publications (35 journal articles and 16 conference proceedings, published between 2010 and 2025) were included after screening, retrieval assessment, and expert recommendation. The included publications were thematically analysed using a hybrid deductive-inductive approach. Results Five themes emerged: (1) situation awareness and its measurement and modelling, (2) collective team cognition, learning, and training, (3) human-autonomy teaming and remote collaboration, (4) visualisation and interface design for shared cognition, and (5) maritime applications of distributed cognition. The evidence demonstrates a shift from static, individual-based models toward dynamic, interaction-driven, and system-level accounts, in which team cognition arises from ongoing interactions among human agents, technical artefacts, and environmental constraints. Discussion The findings indicate that shared and distributed situation awareness is central to coordination and safety in remote maritime operations. Key challenges include integrating autonomous systems, designing interfaces that support distributed sensemaking, and reliably measuring team cognition. Enhancing remote maritime safety requires aligning design, training, and regulatory frameworks with the principles of distributed cognition. Future research should prioritise longitudinal and intervention-based validation in real-world operational contexts.

items.title: Testing Large Language Model Agents on the Use of Biological Tools for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening Evasion
items.abstract: This report is a continuation of previous efforts to test the ability of large language model (LLM)-driven artificial intelligence (AI) agents to interface with AI-enabled biological tools (BTs). While rapid advancements in BTs in recent years have brought promise to accelerate scientific discovery, they also raise significant biosecurity concerns about potential misuse. The biosecurity community is particularly interested in the extent to which LLMs can lower technical barriers and assist non-expert users in accessing and operating BTs. Despite this interest, few evaluations have focused on LLM-BT interactions in the context of a defined threat model. To address this gap, this report describes a test of frontier LLM-driven AI Agents on their ability to use BTs to redesign peptides and proteins to evade nucleic acid synthesis screening measures. Highly relevant to biorisk, this task assesses a potential capability of AI agents that could enable a breach of a critical early defensive layer designed to prevent a multitude of biological misuse scenarios. The findings presented here intend to offer a foundation for biosecurity researchers and AI developers to conduct or further risk and capability assessments as these technologies progress.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON THE PLANNING IN SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative catalyst in Supply Chain Management (SCM), shifting operations from traditional models to predictive and automated systems. This article examines the impact of AI technologies—specifically Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), on supply chain planning. Grounded in Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT) and Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), we analyze how AI enhances planning efficiency across strategic, tactical, and operational horizons. Furthermore, we critically evaluate key implementation challenges, including data governance, system integration, algorithmic transparency, human-AI trust, and organizational change management. The article concludes with key managerial insights and future research directions for sustainable, resilient, and AI-augmented supply chains.

items.title: The influence of fatigue on airline pilots and its implications for operational safety
items.abstract: This study analyzes the influence of operational fatigue on airline pilots and copilots operating at a regional airport and its potential impact on aviation safety. Fatigue has been recognized by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) as a critical human factor affecting decision-making, attention, and operational performance in flight operations. The objective of this research is to identify the main factors associated with fatigue among flight crew members and evaluate their relationship with working hours, rest periods, and perceived performance during flight operations. A quantitative, descriptive, and cross-sectional study was conducted using a structured questionnaire applied to airline captains and first officers operating at the local airport. The study population consisted of 112 airline pilots, from which a sample of 41 participants was obtained. Data were collected over a four-week period during operational schedules associated with higher fatigue risk (04:30–06:00 and 22:00–01:00). The survey evaluated variables including working hours, rest periods, sleep quality, fatigue symptoms, and perceived operational performance. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistical methods, including frequency distributions and percentage analysis. The results indicate that a considerable proportion of participants reported symptoms associated with fatigue, including drowsiness, reduced concentration, and decreased alertness during flight operations, particularly during night operations and after extended working hours. Additionally, irregular rest cycles and high operational workload were identified as key factors contributing to fatigue among pilots. The findings highlight the importance of implementing fatigue mitigation strategies and strengthening Fatigue Risk Management Systems (FRMS) within airline operations. This study contributes to the understanding of fatigue as a multidimensional human factor that can influence pilot performance and aviation safety.

items.title: The Invisible Employer: Algorithmic Management and the Reinvention of Control in the Gig Economy
items.abstract: Every employment relationship in labour law has, until now, presupposed a visible employer — a person or entity capable of being identified, questioned, and held to account for the direction it exercises over a worker. The gig economy disturbs this premise. Platforms exercise the same functions traditionally associated with an employer — assigning work, setting pay, monitoring performance, and terminating access — not through a visible supervisor but through an algorithm whose rules the worker cannot see and cannot contest. This paper asks whether the traditional control test, built on the assumption of an identifiable, human directing mind, can meaningfully regulate a relationship in which the employer’s authority has become functionally invisible, and if not, how the law should respond. The paper adopts a doctrinal and comparative method. It examines how platforms use ratings, personalised pay, gamification and automated deactivation to manage workers in ride-hailing, delivery and freelance work, and places this alongside the legislative and ballot-driven contest over worker status in California under Assembly Bill 5 and Proposition 22, and the European Union’s 2024 Platform Work Directive, which introduces a rebuttable presumption of employment triggered by defined indicators of algorithmic direction and control. The paper argues that algorithmic management does not eliminate employer control but relocates and conceals it, replacing a visible supervisor with an opaque system that performs the same disciplinary function while evading the doctrinal tests designed to detect it. The paper concludes that the law and workers alike need better tools to hold the invisible employer to account, starting with meaningful access for workers to the criteria used to evaluate and pay them and human review of automated decisions with serious consequences, such as deactivation.

items.title: The mediating role of AI anxiety between AI literacy and attitudes towards AI in nursing students: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: AI is a key driver in the Fourth Industrial Revolution, significantly impacting healthcare. Nursing students’ acceptance and readiness to use AI are crucial for its successful integration. Understanding their perceptions is vital to prepare them for the intelligent healthcare era. To examine the mediation effect of AI anxiety between AI literacy and attitudes towards AI in college nursing students. A cross-sectional study. Nursing students from 10 universities across 7 provinces in China were recruited using convenience sampling from May to June 2025. The data collection tools included the Self-Designed Demographic Questionnaire, the General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale and the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale. Data were collated and analyzed using SPSS Statistics 26.0 software and AMOS 29.0 software. The study found that nursing students possess moderate levels of AI literacy and AI anxiety, while generally maintaining positive attitudes towards AI. Mediation analysis indicated that AI anxiety statistically mediated the association between AI literacy and nursing students’ attitudes towards AI. AI literacy was significantly associated with nursing students’ attitudes towards AI, and AI anxiety statistically mediated this association. Therefore, nursing education may benefit from a dual-path approach, designed to simultaneously enhance cognitive competencies (AI literacy) and manage affective responses (AI anxiety).

items.title: The Next Language of Biology May Not Be Human
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing how cancer biology is read, searched, modeled, and turned into hypotheses. But scientific AI does not meet biology directly. Much of what it learns has already passed through English, abstracts, pathway labels, database entries, and text-mined relations. New foundation models create a second translation problem. They can learn from molecular structures, single-cell profiles, perturbation data, and clinical trajectories without first converting those relations into human-readable explanations. This could expand biological and biomedical discovery, but it also changes the burden of proof. If a model proposes a target, biomarker, stratification, or perturbation that is reproducible but only partly interpretable, what evidence should be required before researchers or clinicians act on it? We argue that interpretability is not only an engineering problem. It is a translation problem. When the internal language of a model is difficult to read, the external evidence must become stronger: clear provenance, experimental challenge, cross-population validation, reproducibility, and accountable human judgment.

items.title: The Potential Impacts of Artificial Intelligence on Preoperative Optimization and Predicting Risks of Morbidity and Mortality: A Narrative Focused Review
items.abstract: Preoperative optimization clinics enhance surgical outcomes by optimizing patients' health, reducing unnecessary tests, and minimizing cancellations. Artificial intelligence (AI) now promises to further advance these efforts by improving predictive modeling, automating risk assessments, and enabling personalized care strategies. AI models have shown particular strength in predicting postoperative complications, such as cardiovascular events. Tools like natural language processing (NLP) have also improved risk detection for conditions like alcohol misuse. The historical development of preoperative clinics-from Dr. J Alfred Lee's initial concept in 1949 to modern models like Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) and Anesthesia Preoperative Evaluation Clinic (APEC)-laid the groundwork for today's integration of electronic health records (EHRs) and decision-support systems, now evolving toward AI-driven care. Machine-learning algorithms have proven superior to traditional models for predicting postoperative anemia, opioid dependence, diabetes complications, and mortality risks, thus offering precise stratification and resource optimization. Specific applications include AI-assisted anemia management, penicillin allergy delabelling, and opioid use prediction after major surgeries. AI also enhances patient education through tools like ChatGPT and improves smoking cessation efforts using conversational AI. NLP has demonstrated better accuracy than standard International Classification of Disease (ICD) codes in identifying risky alcohol use (>2 standard drinks per day before surgery). However, barriers to widespread adoption include data privacy, algorithmic bias, and clinician skepticism. Future studies should focus on validating AI models across diverse populations and integrating AI recommendations within clinical workflows while adhering to evolving regulatory standards. Ultimately, AI's incorporation into preoperative assessments could significantly boost the efficiency and impact of clinic resources, potentially shifting outcomes more favorably by improving the slope of resource utilization versus patient outcome curves. Continued research and refinement are essential for AI to achieve its full potential in perioperative medicine.

items.title: The Remote Work Paradox: Why Flexibility Raises Retention—and Why Poor Design Destroys Collaboration
items.abstract: Remote work has become one of the most consequential and contested organizational changes of the modern workplace. Yet discussions about remote and hybrid work are often reduced to a binary disagreement between advocates of employee flexibility and leaders who prioritize office attendance. This working paper argues that the central question is not whether remote work universally succeeds or fails. The more useful question is which combinations of tasks, employees, managerial practices, communication systems, performance measures, and workplace arrangements allow remote work to produce sustainable value. The paper presents a practitioner-led narrative review of influential field experiments, observational studies, meta-analytic research, and international institutional evidence concerning remote and hybrid work. It examines six major outcome areas: employee productivity, retention, collaboration, professional learning, well-being, and equitable access to opportunity. The evidence indicates that the effects of remote work are heterogeneous rather than universally positive or negative.Research reviewed in the paper shows that remote work can increase measured performance in structured roles with observable outputs, limited task interdependence, and suitable working conditions. Hybrid arrangements can improve employee satisfaction and materially reduce voluntary turnover without reducing performance. Location flexibility can also broaden access to talent, reduce commuting burdens, support caregivers, and enable organizations to recruit beyond their immediate geographic markets. However, remote work can create important organizational costs when it is introduced without an appropriate operating system. Large-scale evidence suggests that firm-wide remote work can make collaboration networks more static and siloed, shift communication toward asynchronous channels, and reduce opportunities for spontaneous cross-team interaction. Distance can also weaken informal mentoring, slow the development of early-career employees, increase coordination costs, blur boundaries between professional and personal life, and expose weaknesses in management that physical proximity previously concealed.To reconcile these competing outcomes, the paper introduces the “remote work paradox”: the same flexibility that improves autonomy, retention, and focused individual work can simultaneously weaken collaboration, shared context, informal learning, and organizational connection. These effects are not mutually exclusive. A company may experience lower employee turnover while its internal collaboration network becomes narrower. An employee may complete more individual tasks while receiving less coaching and having fewer opportunities to form professionally valuable relationships. The paper proposes the REMOTE operating framework as a practical approach for designing and evaluating distributed work. The six dimensions of the framework are Role suitability, Expectation clarity, Managerial cadence, Output evidence, Team connection, and Equitable access. Together, these dimensions reposition remote work as an organizational-design challenge rather than a debate about employee location.Role suitability requires organizations to examine the actual tasks within each position and determine which activities benefit from quiet concentration, which require physical resources, and which depend on rapid coordination or tacit knowledge. Expectation clarity requires written outcomes, ownership, deadlines, quality standards, communication norms, and escalation procedures. Managerial cadence concerns the predictable systems through which managers provide coaching, feedback, prioritization, and workload review. Output evidence requires performance to be assessed through meaningful results rather than online visibility or digital activity. Team connection addresses trust, mentoring, weak ties, shared context, and cross-functional collaboration. Equitable access requires organizations to ensure that remote employees receive fair access to information, important assignments, feedback, sponsorship, compensation, and promotion opportunities. The paper also develops seven propositions that organizations can evaluate using their own operational data. These propositions address task suitability, coordinated hybrid schedules, employee retention, differences between experienced and early-career workers, the value of documentation, the influence of managerial capability, and the risk of proximity bias. The propositions are not presented as newly established causal findings. Instead, they translate the reviewed literature into testable expectations that organizations can use when conducting workplace-policy pilots. A five-stage implementation protocol is presented for employers. Organizations are encouraged to diagnose their work processes, design an explicit location model, pilot the model for a defined period, measure a balanced set of outcomes, and adapt the policy according to the evidence. Recommended measurements include productivity, work quality, cycle time, employee turnover, absenteeism, customer outcomes, collaboration patterns, onboarding progress, feedback latency, workload, employee experience, and equity across demographic and location groups. The paper concludes that remote work should be understood as an organizational technology whose value depends on complementary investments in management, documentation, communication, cybersecurity, job design, performance measurement, and inclusive employment practices. The strongest remote-work policy is neither the most permissive nor the most restrictive. It is the policy that makes productive work easier, learning faster, accountability clearer, collaboration more intentional, and professional opportunity more equitable.

items.title: The Reported Engagement with AI Level (REAL) Rating: A Framework for Disclosing Human-AI Collaboration
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly incorporated into digital media and more generally into production workflows with which the public frequently interacts. Current provenance standards and disclosure methods frequently rely on binary categorizations, differentiating only between entirely human-authored and AI-generated content, or depend on technical watermarking that lacks user-facing clarity. However, there are very different risks and outcomes depending on the different uses of AI in the creation and consumption of end products. Therefore, we propose the Reported Engagement with AI Level (REAL) Rating framework which addresses these concerns by introducing a six-tier scale (Levels 0-5) that discloses the extent of AI involvement in both product creation and user experience. This paper details the structural methodology of the REAL Rating system and the specifics of its application across text, image, audio, video, and software products.

items.title: The Role Of Artificial Intelligence In Transforming Financial Accounting And Tax Compliance
items.abstract: The role of artificial intelligence (AI) in transforming financial accounting and tax compliance is one of those areas that have become very intricate in terms of regulation. Based on the systematic review and synthesis of recent empirical research and industry surveys (2021–2026), the study evaluates how AI, including machine learning, natural language processing, and generative AI, transforms essential accounting and tax processes. As follows, the implementation of AI technologies leads to efficiency gains, including 81% productivity increases and the enhancement of accuracy up to 98%. Companies using AI-powered compliance solutions attain the accuracy rate in fraud detection of more than 98%, while the processing time is reduced to less than a second. However, despite numerous benefits, there are still some challenges identified, including the lack of appropriate internal skills among 44% of respondents and low data readiness among 80% of respondents. Thus, the paper concludes that effective application of AI technologies is possible only through effective collaboration between humans and AI and appropriate governance, which requires significant investments into data infrastructure.

items.title: Trajectory-Derived Confidence for Reliable, Resource-Aware Clinical Text-to-SQL Agents
items.abstract: LLM agents for clinical text-to-SQL applications reason autonomously over multiple steps but cannot assess whether their own reasoning or outputs can be trusted. In high leverage applications such as healthcare, this presents a critical risk where system mistakes can be costly. These reliability failures are also resource failures: an incorrect reasoning trajectory spends computation budget on outputs that must be discarded. We introduce Sentinel, a trajectory-derived, classifier-based confidence layer that analyzes an agent's reasoning, code and database outputs to decide at three points whether to stop: refusing unanswerable questions before the agent runs, halting doomed trajectories mid-run, and withholding untrustworthy answers at delivery. Here, utilizing Chow's rule, we optimize decisions under the EHRSQL shared task's Reliability Score, which penalizes incorrect answers given a utility weighting, and find on the benchmark EHRSQL that Sentinel raises this score from +0.08 to +0.24 when mistakes have a low utility weighting, well above the +0.03 earned by refusing every question, with delivered-answer accuracy rising from 54% to 69% as coverage falls from 84% to 55%. At higher stakes the agents we test rarely answer reliably enough to deliver, and Sentinel detects this on its own, abstaining to that same +0.03 where the unmonitored agent scores -3.02. The same stopping decisions cut computation: at low stakes, where the system still answers, Sentinel eliminates 13-28% of agent steps at little or no reliability cost.

items.title: UNLEASHING HARMONIOUS GREEN PASSION IN HOSPITALITY ENTERPRISES: A MODERATED-MEDIATED ROLE OF PRO-ENVIRONMENTAL BEHAVIOR AND GREEN ORGANIZATIONAL CLIMATE
items.abstract: Environmental sustainability in the hospitality sector increasingly depends on the alignment between employees’ intrinsic motivations, supportive organizational contexts, and environmentally responsible behaviors. Drawing on SelfDetermination Theory, this study examines how Harmonious Green Passion influences environmental performance in Egypt’s five-star hotels, focusing on the mediating role of pro-environmental behavior and the moderating effect of green organizational climate. Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of 402 hotel employees and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling. The findings demonstrate that Harmonious Green Passion positively influences both proenvironmental behavior and environmental performance, while pro-environmental behavior partially mediates the relationship between Harmonious Green Passion and environmental performance. Furthermore, green organizational climate significantly strengthens the positive relationship between Harmonious Green Passion and pro-environmental behavior, consequently reinforcing its indirect effect on environmental performance. These findings extend Self-Determination Theory by elucidating a motivation–behavior–performance mechanism through which employees’ environmentally oriented passion translates into organizational outcomes, while demonstrating that this process is contingent upon contextual organizational conditions. Practically, the findings suggest that hotel managers should cultivate supportive green organizational climates, encourage employees’ intrinsic environmental motivation, and facilitate pro-environmental behaviors through appropriate organizational practices. Such efforts can strengthen employees’ environmental engagement and contribute to improved environmental performance, offering hospitality organizations a pathway toward more sustainable operations and long-term environmental value creation.

items.title: Use of AI tools among allied healthcare students: Academic integrity, online learning integrity, and nomophobia as predictors
items.abstract: The swift convergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), online instruction, and mobile dependence has transformed higher education, introducing both innovations and ethical problems for allied health training. Although individual studies on AI adoption, digital ethics, and device dependence exist, a significant empirical gap remains regarding how psychological reliance on mobile devices (nomophobia) and virtual-specific ethics jointly drive GenAI adoption among healthcare students, where ethical lapses directly impact clinical competence. To address this gap, this study examined the predictive roles of academic integrity, online learning integrity, and nomophobia in the use of AI tools among allied healthcare students at a higher education institution. Employing a quantitative cross-sectional design, the researchers collected data via convenience sampling among 300 full-time allied health students in Central Luzon, Philippines. The study used four research tools to gather pertinent data for the investigation, including an online survey administered during the second semester of the 2025-2026 academic year. Both descriptive and inferential statistics were employed using SPSS 23. Descriptive results showed high academic integrity, moderate AI usage and nomophobia, but low online learning integrity. Correlation analyses showed that AI tool use was positively associated with online learning integrity, nomophobia, and academic integrity. Multiple linear regression demonstrated that the model significantly predicted AI usage. Online learning integrity was the strongest predictor, followed by academic integrity and nomophobia. These results show that ethical digital engagement and mobile connectedness actively propel AI integration; ultimately, achieving SDG 4 objectives within healthcare education requires moving beyond prohibitive policies toward anticipatory digital governance, robust AI literacy, and ethical models that prepare future professionals for a digitally driven medical environment.

items.title: Validation of a Questionnaire to Explore Artificial Intelligence Use Among Upper-Secondary and Higher Education Teachers
items.abstract: Research on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education has shifted from students to teachers, yet available teacher instruments rest on technology acceptance models, professional knowledge frameworks, or AI literacy, and none articulates dispositional conditions, teaching activities, and contextual consequences within a single functional logic. This study extends to teachers an instrument previously validated with students and grounded in Functional Behavior Analysis and the Interbehavioral Model of Didactic Performance. Participants were 233 Mexican upper-secondary and higher education teachers (mean age 47.22 years, SD = 10.44). The study is strictly psychometric in scope: it reports initial reliability and internal structure evidence, not a profile of teacher practice. Reliability was estimated with Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega with bootstrap confidence intervals, and the number of components was determined through Horn’s parallel analysis. Alpha coefficients ranged from 0.703 to 0.957 (omega, 0.755 to 0.962). The benefits dimension split into two uncorrelated components, pedagogical benefits (α = 0.953) and risks to academic integrity (α = 0.771). Domains of didactic performance proved unidimensional (63.0% of variance); the consequences dimension behaved as a formative index rather than a reflective scale; and the dispositional dimension failed to separate individual from contextual variables and required redesign. A second-order analysis yielded two orthogonal axes, favourable pedagogical orientation and risk recognition, on which four quadrants are described for illustrative purposes only. The instrument discriminates across self-reported frequency of AI use. Because components were extracted from Pearson correlations on ordinal items in a single convenience sample, the structure reported here is provisional and requires confirmation with polychoric matrices and robust estimators on an independent sample.

items.title: What Is Lost in Post-Training? Default Collapse and the Loss of In-Context Steerability Across Diverse Perspectives
items.abstract: AI models serving a heterogeneous population must act on the principles appropriate to each user and context. While post-training has been shown to narrow the views large language models express, prior work has focused on default behavior rather than the ability to adapt to in-context information. We show that post-training also degrades a model's ability to be steered in-context toward perspectives it was not trained to favor. In controlled experiments, we fine-tune models toward one side of cultural-value disagreements and evaluate checkpoints throughout training. The trained side becomes increasingly dominant in ordinary use, while the ability to recognize and faithfully enact the opposing view declines. These findings point to a tension between prioritizing a single set of values and preserving the technical capacity needed to serve diverse stakeholders. Finally, we propose and analyze an alternative objective that maximizes reward subject to a prescribed distribution over expressed perspectives, and present stance-distribution matching as a practical implementation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: When Numbers Start Talking: Numerical Signalling and Strategic Behaviour Among LLMs
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly operate in multi-agent systems (MAS) characterised by strategic interaction. However, little is known about whether, and to what extent, different types of messages affect the outcomes of strategic games. By investigating AI agents based on four popular LLMs, playing four games with different cooperation equilibria, we study whether messages of different kinds (natural language, numerical signals, or random sequences) significantly modify the levels of cooperation in each game, also depending on the agents' assigned personalities. We observe that structured messages alter the final payoffs for most games and LLMs, but without a predictable pattern; this challenges the assumption that AI agents can converge to stable equilibria regardless of additional capabilities. Moreover, we observe that agent-generated numerical messages depart from randomness, most strongly and consistently when agents are explicitly instructed to communicate; however, they introduce an additional interpretability challenge, as their symbol distributions are mostly associated with the payoff structure and typically become more concentrated with repetition, but are overall difficult for humans to interpret. Monitoring for coordination of AI agents through restricted channels should thus prioritise message-level fingerprints, which generalise across models, over behavioural decisions, which do not.

items.abstract: This presentation summarizes the 90 Days of Research Visibility® initiative, a practical framework that shows researchers how to use artificial intelligence (AI) to build a consistent, authentic, and discoverable personal research presence. It highlights practical approaches for strengthening academic identity and digital presence, transforming research publications into engaging content, and communicating research effectively to audiences beyond academia. The presentation also examines how AI-assisted tools can help researchers improve research discoverability, visibility, engagement, and overall impact across academic and professional platforms. Drawing on lessons and practical activities from the 90-day initiative, the session provides an accessible roadmap for researchers and faculty members to integrate AI into their research communication and visibility workflows while maintaining human judgment, authenticity, and academic integrity.

items.title: A Comparative Explainability Framework for DeBERTa-v3 in Zero-Shot Medical Abstract Classification
items.abstract: A comparative explainability framework is presented to audit DeBERTa-v3 under zero-shot classification of medical abstracts. The work addresses the disagreement problem in Explainable Artificial Intelligence, where different attribution methods produce divergent explanations for the same input and prediction. A natural language inference engine is implemented over the Medical Abstracts corpus with five enriched hypotheses per diagnostic category and a balanced sample of one thousand texts per class. Five explanation methods are compared: SHAP and LIME as model-agnostic approaches, occlusion and Input x Gradient as deep-learning-specific approaches, and Attention x Gradient as a transformer-specific approach. Explanations are standardized through top-token attribution, and pairwise agreement is quantified using the Jaccard index. High predictive accuracy is achieved across well-defined clinical domains, whereas performance degrades under high semantic ambiguity. Explanatory stability directly mirrors predictive certainty, exhibiting strong convergence in univalent categories and a marked drop under diagnostic uncertainty. Furthermore, qualitative error auditing uncovers three systemic failure mechanisms: lexical hypersensitivity, semantic overlap, and loss of attribution coherence. The results support the combined use of several explanation methods and quantitative agreement metrics when auditing transformer-based models in medical text classification, and suggest prioritizing specific clinical ontologies over broad diagnostic labels.

items.title: A Design Theory for AI-Assisted Software Development Derived from Christopher Alexander's Theory of Form
items.abstract: Code generated by large language models (LLMs) cannot be assumed to meet specified requirements. Reviews, testing, and static analysis still apply, but which of them a sufficient harness needs, and in what role, is open. We propose a design theory derived from Christopher Alexander's theory of form, and a methodology for applying it. In Alexander's account, fit between a form and its context can be perceived only negatively, through the absence of identified misfits. We make the organization's tradition explicit and derive the misfits from it and from the problem's classification. The theory models the LLM as a non-native vernacular builder, trained on many codebases but native to none, whose output tends to drift toward mainstream conventions rather than the local tradition. We engineer four pieces of machinery: explicit representations of the problem (Jackson's problem frames) and of the tradition (a four-form pattern language); deterministic misfit detectors; a fix loop; and a human-gated legislative circuit governing the representations and detectors. We call the resulting methodology, a practice of harness engineering, Misfit-Governed Development (MGD). Its dual-loop process separates an autonomous inner loop, where the LLM iterates against the gates, from a human outer loop, where specifications are judged against the world. Together they form the S = P = T = W assurance model (specification, program, tests, world), whose equals signs name relations, not identity. We report evidence from building and rebuilding a Scrum system of four event-sourced aggregates from 64 problem-frame specifications, verified by about 1,300 generated tests and 28 blocking gates, one applying 188 rules. This addresses the generativity dimension of Alexander's 1996 OOPSLA challenge. The moral dimension, whether the specification still fits the world, requires human judgment and belongs to the outer loop.

items.title: A Deterministic and Auditable AI Security Risk Assessment Framework with ATLAS Aligned Executable Rules and Formal Verification
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in high impact and safety critical settings, yet security assessment remains difficult to reproduce and defend under audit. Existing approaches often rely on narrative checklists or assessor driven scoring, and they lack an explicit, machine evaluable mapping from observable engineering artefacts to stable technique level outcomes. We present an evidence driven AI security assessment framework that operationalises assessment as a deterministic decision function. The framework normalises heterogeneous artefacts into a project independent Control ID taxonomy scored on a bounded four level ordinal scale, compiles technique level predicates from a pinned MITRE ATLAS snapshot via an explicit mitigation to control mapping, and outputs technique indexed feasibility and impact levels with traceable links back to the triggering evidence. We package all normative choices as a versioned assessment policy object to support repeatable reassessment across snapshots. To ensure semantic correctness, we formally verify boundedness, totality, ordered semantic consistency, and monotonicity of the compiled evaluator over the full declared score domain. items.title: A Lean–Six Sigma–Ergonomics Index for Assessing Shop-Floor Operational Resilience Readiness: Method Development and SME Demonstration
items.abstract: Operational resilience readiness at the shop-floor level depends on efficient process flow, stable quality, and adequate human–system capacity, yet these dimensions are commonly assessed separately. This article presents the Lean–Six Sigma–Ergonomics Operational Resilience Index (LSE–ORI), a non-interventional composite method for assessing manufacturing conditions that support resilience readiness. Process-flow efficiency is represented by Process Cycle Efficiency, quality stability by the actual sigma level normalized against a defined target, and human–system capacity by physical, cognitive, and macroergonomic assessments. The scores are standardized to a 0–1 scale and combined multiplicatively to produce the index and identify the lowest-scoring dimension. A two-month demonstration involving 13 operators on a tractor spare-parts production line yielded scores of 0.60, 0.54, and 0.62, resulting in an ORI of approximately 0.20. Quality stability was the lowest-scoring primary component, while work-system structural support was the weakest subcomponent within the human–system. Content validation by 15 experts across 64 items produced a minimum I-CVI of 0.933 and an S-CVI/Ave of 0.995, supporting applicability, calculation traceability, and content validity. Main advantages of the proposed method: • Integrates three shop-floor dimensions into one assessment. • Uses operational data without changing the production system. Provides hierarchical diagnosis of the lowest-scoring component.

items.title: A Literature Review on Workplace Spirituality, Work-Life Balance, and Employee Performance (2020-2025)
items.abstract: Modern workplace transformation driven by technological connectivity, flexible work systems, and increasing job demands has intensified challenges related to employee well-being and organizational performance. In this context, workplace spirituality and work–life balance have emerged as important organizational dimensions associated with employee attitudes, psychological well-being, and work outcomes. This study aims to systematically review empirical literature examining the relationships among workplace spirituality, work–life balance, and employee performance published between 2020 and 2025. This review employed the PRISMA 2020 framework to ensure a transparent and systematic review process. Relevant studies were identified through searches in Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using predefined keywords related to workplace spirituality, work–life balance, and employee performance. Inclusion criteria were limited to peer-reviewed empirical journal articles published in English between 2020 and 2025. Following the identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion stages, a total of 10 studies were included in the final synthesis and analyzed using thematic synthesis. The review findings indicate that workplace spirituality is commonly associated with employee engagement, organizational commitment, intrinsic motivation, and meaningful work experiences. Work–life balance was likewise associated with higher job satisfaction, lower occupational stress, and more favorable employee performance outcomes. Several studies also highlighted the mediating roles of emotional intelligence and organizational commitment in these relationships. Overall, the synthesis suggests that supportive spiritual values and balanced work practices are associated with improved employee performance and psychological well-being within contemporary organizational settings.

items.abstract: Abstract The article illuminates the communicative power of graphic novels and the instructional rationale for their use for health professions education (HPE), particularly for enhancing critical thinking, empathy, and interpersonal skills. The article also provides a methodological framework for creating graphic novels that incorporates Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for narrative codification and visual synthesis. It outlines a two-phase process: Phase I (Architecture), focused on conceptual design, and Phase II (Construction), which utilizes a "Human-AI-Human" (H-AI-H) workflow to streamline production while maintaining pedagogical integrity.

items.title: ActiveSaddler: Automated Curriculum Learning for Agent Harness Optimization
items.abstract: Automated harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents by iteratively updating their prompts, tool interfaces, and control logic from execution feedback. However, existing methods primarily optimize how the harness is updated while largely fixing which training scenarios generate the feedback that drives those updates. As the harness evolves, the scenarios most useful for further optimization can change, suggesting that the training curriculum itself should adapt alongside the harness. We formulate this missing dimension of harness optimization as an automated curriculum learning problem and introduce ActiveSaddler. ActiveSaddler models the evolving curriculum as a non-stationary bandit with dynamically instantiated optimization targets. It abstracts recurring failures into reusable failure-pattern arms, estimates the potential learning progress from further targeting each pattern, and adaptively balances revisiting known weaknesses with exploring unseen scenarios for new ones. Optimization outcomes continually update both the set of discovered failure patterns and their priorities, allowing the curriculum to co-evolve with the harness. Experiments on GAIA2 and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that ActiveSaddler consistently discovers stronger harnesses, improving test Pass@1 by 4.4 and 7.5 percentage points over the same harness optimizer using a scenario order fixed before optimization, respectively. Ablations further show that these gains depend on dynamically constructing optimization targets, estimating their evolving utility, and balancing continued optimization with new failure discovery. Together, these results establish automated curriculum learning as a new crucial optimization dimension for harness optimization.

items.title: ADHD and Work–Life Spillover: An Empirical Study of How Workplace Demands Influence Personal Relationships and Well-Being
items.abstract: Design/methodology/approach- 420 working adult Indians were surveyed cross-sectionally, 84 (20.0) met the descriptive ADHD-group requirement with an ASRS-5 score of 14 or above on the survey. Workplace demands, ADHD-related functioning (ASRS-5), emotional dysregulation (DERS-16), work-life spillover, relationship quality, well-being (WH-5) and perceived stress (PSS-10) were the established tools to assess organizational functioning. Hierarchical multiple regression, moderation analysis and bootstrapped moderated mediation analysis were used to test hypothesis using PROCESS. Results- The workplace needs were positively correlated with work-life spillover (8.53, p =.001). Workplace-demands X ASRS-5 interaction (=.17, p =.001) and place of work-demands X DERS-16 interaction (=.21, p <.001) were significant. Spillover had a negative correlation with relationship quality (= -.46, p <.001) and well-being (= -.49, p <.001) and a positive correlation with the perceived stress (=.52, p <.001). The bootstrapped indirect effects were significant in all three results, and the moderators’ indices were significant in both moderators. Findings – Workplace demands had a positive relationship with work-life spillover (W =.51, p = -.001) in the results. The workplace-demands times ASRS-5 point of contact (=.17, p =.001) and the workplace-demands times DERS-16 (=.21, p =.001) was significant. Relationship quality (β = -.46, p <.001) and well-being (β = -.49, p <.001) were negatively related to spillover, and perceived stress was positively (β =.52, p <.001) related to spillover. All three outcomes had significant bootstrapped indirect effects and significant indices of moderated mediation with both moderators. Practical implications - The results guide job design, workload anticipations and facilitation of workers whose attentional and emotional control at work is burdensome to maintain. Originality/value - The research not only investigates the ADHD issue in the workplace but the cross-domain pathway developed, taking ADHD as a dimensional and demonstrates how the impact of the condition diffuses out of work in personal life.

items.title: Affective governance theory: rethinking organisational control in digitally mediated organisations
items.abstract: Digital work is increasingly organised through communication platforms, workflow systems, electronic monitoring and algorithmic systems. Existing research already shows that digital technologies create affordances, structure choice, intensify visibility and support algorithmic and datafication-based control. The unresolved issue is therefore not whether digital systems influence behaviour, but how recurrent digital cues become organisationally linked to norms and anticipated consequences strongly enough to acquire stable affective and evaluative force. This paper formulates Affective Governance Theory (AGT) as a new mid-range theory of organisational control. Using an abductive conceptual model-building approach, the analysis integrates organisational control, digital affordances and sociomateriality, algorithmic and datafication control, digital nudging and persuasive technology, surveillance, affect theory and work-design scholarship. Theory development proceeds through anomaly specification, comparison of alternative explanations, iterative construct formation, discriminant and boundary testing, and recursive model derivation. AGT proposes that digital work infrastructures become affective configurations when four conditions co-occur: recurrent dependence, evaluative legibility, organisational norm linkage and anticipated relational or professional consequences. Three mutually reinforcing mechanisms, affective inscription, anticipatory self-regulation and the moral economy of digital presence, explain how these configurations orient behaviour and become recursively reproduced. Seven propositions specify emergence, operation, discriminant effects, sustainable-work consequences and structural amplification. AGT does not claim that digital design, monitoring or algorithms shaping behaviour are new. Its contribution is to theorise the organisational conversion of recurrent digital affordances into relatively stable affective governance structures and to generate predictions that can be tested against surveillance, algorithmic control, nudging and normative control. Practically, AGT offers a diagnostic for identifying when digital work design turns visibility, response latency and online presence into informal governance demands. It thereby connects responsible digital transformation with employee autonomy, recovery, dignity, well-being and equity.

items.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Food Science: A Conceptual Framework and Structured Synthesis for Food Safety, Shelf-Life Extension, and Environmental Sustainability
items.abstract: The global food system faces three converging pressures. Foodborne diseases affect an estimated 600 million people each year. Post-harvest losses and waste exceed 30% of total production. Food systems also generate roughly one-quarter to one-third of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions. Existing artificial intelligence (AI) tools address these pressures only in isolation. Most are narrow, task-specific predictive models. They classify, forecast, or flag. They do not perceive, reason, and act within a single closed loop. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that closes that loop. We define agentic AI as autonomous software entities that perceive their environment, reason over causal and physical models, and execute bounded actions under explicit governance. The framework has three layers: Perception, Reasoning, and Action. A Digital Twin sits at the reasoning core. It simulates candidate interventions before any physical action is taken. The framework is supported by a structured literature synthesis rather than a systematic meta-analysis and we also document the searched databases, search strings, screening steps, and inclusion criteria. All quantitative values reported in this paper are presented as indicative ranges with explicit provenance tags. Each value is labeled by evidence tier: field deployment, laboratory testing, simulation, or secondary literature. No new field trials were conducted for this study. The performance figures should therefore be read as reported potential, not as validated outcomes. The contributions of this work are fourfold. First, we specify a unified Perception–Reasoning–Action architecture that integrates Digital Twins for closed-loop food system optimization. Second, we provide a critical synthesis of prior literature, a source-by-source evidence traceability matrix, and a benchmarking scheme that compares agentic AI against task-specific baselines rather than a single homogeneous baseline. Third, we propose a tiered governance model mapped explicitly to HACCP, ISO 22000, FDA guidance, and the EU AI Act, including an accountability allocation for autonomous food-safety decisions. Fourth, we operationalize Socio-Technical Systems theory into an adoption framework and a staged validation agenda for future empirical work.

items.title: AgentInspect: Diagnosing Behavioral Failures in Artificial Intelligence Agents
items.abstract: Effectively testing Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents remains a fundamental challenge due to their stochastic reasoning, vast and diverse input space, reliance on external tools, and operation in dynamic execution environments; factors that demand new testing methodologies explicitly tailored to the complex and interactive nature of agent-based systems. This work presents a novel methodology for testing AI agents, with a particular focus on assessing their behavioral robustness under varied operational conditions. Our approach relies on following key technical innovations: (1) a coverage-guided test input generation strategy based on agent- specific coverage objectives, (2) a capture-and-simulate mechanism that systematically emulates abnormal tool behaviors to mimic real-world execution failures, and (3) a deterministic behavioral failure detection approach that enables consistent identification of failures across different test inputs. We developed AgentInspect, a framework that automatically detects six types of behavioral failures in LangChain-based AI agents by analyzing their execution trajectories across three evaluation settings: a baseline setting using real tool responses, a simulated setting incorporating synthetic tool responses, and a hybrid setting that combines the real and simulated tool responses. To evaluate our approach, we curated a benchmark of 35 AI agents obtained from GitHub. Our results show that AgentInspect consistently identifies different behavioral failures with high precision and recall across all three execution settings. In particular, the simulated and hybrid settings expose failure modes that do not emerge during baseline execution with real tool responses, thereby enabling a more comprehensive assessment of agent robustness. Our findings highlight AgentInspect’s effectiveness in revealing critical failures and its practical utility for systematic robustness evaluation of AI agents.

items.abstract: This study examines the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Supply Chain Management (SCM) among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Lebanon's Food and Beverage (F&B) sector.Using a qualitative approach based on 45 semi-structured interviews, it explores the drivers, barriers, and strategic implications of AI adoption.Even though AI technologies offer significant opportunities, adoption remains uneven especially among SMEs.The findings reveal that participants recognize AI's potential to improve efficiency and competitiveness.Participants reported that AI enhances operational efficiency, cost optimization, and decision support.On the other hand, AI adoption remains limited by technical barriers, financial constraints, skill shortages, and low trust.Based on the Technology Organization Environment (TOE) framework, the Resource-Based View (RBV), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Institutional Theory, the study highlights that successful AI integration depends on several factors.These factors include technological readiness, organizational capabilities, managerial acceptance, and institutional pressures.It suggests enhancing digital infrastructure, developing human capital, and improving governance frameworks to support SMEs.

items.title: AI AND BIG DATA IN HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOUR
items.abstract: the workforce generates more data than ever before. Human resource information systems, applicant tracking platforms, learning systems, engagement surveys, collaboration tools and connected devices record who employees are, what they do, whom they work with and how they feel about their work. Combined with artificial intelligence (AI), this data opens new possibilities for understanding and managing people and organisations. This chapter examines the role of AI and big data in human resource management (HRM) and organisational behaviour (OB), with particular emphasis on people analytics as an organisational capability and on the analysis of behaviour at the level of teams, networks, culture and the organisation as a whole. It traces the evolution from HR metrics to people analytics, identifies the principal sources of workforce data, and explains the analytical methods used, including HR metrics, statistical and survival models, machine learning, text analytics, organisational network analysis and controlled experiments. It reviews applications across the talent lifecycle and in emerging areas such as skills-based talent management, internal talent marketplaces, diversity and inclusion analytics and hybrid work. The chapter then examines how big data is transforming the study and management of organisational behaviour, including collaboration, team effectiveness, leadership, culture and change, and discusses the evidence on the value of people analytics, the barriers to its adoption and its ethical risks. Frameworks for building people analytics capability are presented, followed by a discussion of the Indian context and future directions.

items.title: AI feedback-seeking and learning engagement in art education: psychological antecedents and reflective mechanisms
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence provides students with a feedback source that differs from traditional teacher and peer interaction, yet limited research has explained why students actively seek feedback from AI or how such feedback-seeking is associated with subsequent learning engagement. Drawing on transactional stress and coping theory and social cognitive theory, this study examined the psychological antecedents and reflective mechanisms of AI feedback-seeking in art education. Methods Two complementary studies were conducted. Study 1 utilized survey data from 315 higher education students with recent experience in art learning and generative AI use to investigate whether a fear of negative evaluation was associated with AI feedback-seeking through interpersonal help-seeking avoidance. Study 2 involved 172 students who completed a standardized AI-supported art-creation task. It examined whether AI feedback-seeking was associated with task behavioral engagement through reflective learning and whether openness strengthened this indirect relationship. The proposed relationships were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Results In Study 1, fear of negative evaluation was positively associated with interpersonal help-seeking avoidance, which in turn was associated with greater AI feedback-seeking. The indirect association between fear of negative evaluation and AI feedback-seeking through interpersonal help-seeking avoidance was significant, whereas the direct association was not. In Study 2, AI feedback-seeking was positively associated with reflective learning, which was further associated with task behavioral engagement. Reflective learning significantly mediated the association between AI feedback-seeking and task behavioral engagement. Openness strengthened both the association between AI feedback-seeking and reflective learning and the corresponding indirect association with task behavioral engagement. Discussion The findings indicate that avoiding interpersonal help does not necessarily reflect withdrawal from feedback. Under evaluation concerns, students may instead select AI as a feedback source involving less interpersonal exposure. However, seeking AI feedback is not uniformly associated with stronger learning engagement; its relevance depends on whether students reflect on the information obtained and remain receptive to alternative perspectives. The study positions AI feedback-seeking as both a coping-oriented form of feedback-source selection and a learner-initiated resource for reflective engagement in art education.

items.title: AI integration in STEM learning in inclusive schools in Indonesia from teachers experiences and perspectives
items.abstract: Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in STEM learning within inclusive schools presents a significant opportunity to enhance personalized, adaptive, and equitable learning experiences for diverse learners. However, its successful implementation is constrained by complex pedagogical, technological, and human factors, where teacher perception plays a decisive role. This research aims to analyze the influence of AI integration and teachers’ professional experience on teacher perceptions regarding the use of AI in inclusive STEM education in Indonesia, a context characterized by heterogeneous student needs and varying levels of technological readiness. Employing a quantitative approach with an explanatory survey design, the study involved 1,000 teachers from inclusive primary and secondary schools selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model evaluation confirmed strong psychometric properties, with all indicators meeting validity and reliability criteria (outer loading > 0.70, composite reliability > 0.90, and average variance extracted > 0.50). Structural model results demonstrated that AI integration (β = 0.399, p < 0.001) and teachers’ experience (β = 0.512, p < 0.001) significantly influenced teacher perceptions, with teachers’ experience emerging as the more dominant predictor. The model exhibited moderate explanatory power (R² = 0.449) and excellent goodness of fit (SRMR = 0.045). Furthermore, PLS-Predict analysis indicated high out-of-sample predictive capability, confirming the robustness of the proposed model. These findings underscore that teachers’ lived pedagogical experiences, rather than technological availability alone, are central in shaping constructive perceptions of AI use. Consequently, this study recommends a strategic policy shift from infrastructure-centered initiatives toward sustained, experiential, and inclusive professional development programs to empower teachers in leveraging AI for effective and equitable STEM learning in inclusive educational settings.

items.title: AI Topics Module 2: Education
items.abstract: This textbook module examines the intersection of cognitive neuroscience, pedagogy, and artificial intelligence as they converge in the secondary school classroom. Beginning with the theory of mental rigor — the disciplined, sustained exertion of focused cognitive effort as a biological process with measurable neural correlates — the text argues that understanding how the brain learns and understanding how AI systems learn are not separate intellectual projects but deeply connected ones. Each chapter weaves AI concepts explicitly into its treatment of the neuroscience of learning, establishing structural parallels between biological and artificial intelligence that deepen understanding of both. Chapter One presents culturally responsive classroom activities — including probabilistic choice games, biometric data analysis, memory exercises, and kinesthetic geometry — and connects each to foundational AI concepts including classification, feature engineering, sequence processing, and convolutional neural networks. Chapter Two examines learning environment design alongside AI tools for personalization, adaptive assessment, and classroom analytics, including a critical treatment of their limitations and equity implications. Chapter Three addresses the cultivation of intrinsic motivation through the lens of reinforcement learning, connecting dopaminergic reward circuitry to temporal difference learning and the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. Chapter Four provides a systematic comparison of biological and artificial neural architectures — synaptic plasticity and backpropagation, Piagetian developmental stages and inductive bias, System 1 and System 2 cognition and the symbolic-to-connectionist transition in AI. Chapter Five presents educator roundtable discussions on identity, equity, algorithmic bias, AI-era assessment, school leadership, and asset-based teaching in an AI-integrated educational landscape. The module includes a mathematical appendix connecting classroom activities to the computational foundations of machine learning, and a reference list of 32 peer-reviewed publications spanning cognitive neuroscience, educational psychology, and AI research. It is intended for educators, researchers, educational leaders, policymakers, and students engaged with the rapidly evolving relationship between human learning and artificial intelligence. This is Module 2 in the AI Topics series by Xavier Honablue, M.Ed. Module 1, Epigenetics, is available separately on Zenodo.

items.title: AI Use in Counter Terrorism
items.abstract: Terrorism continues to be one of the most pervasive threats to public safety, societal fear and harmony across the world. Extremist and terrorist perpetrators have always evolved their tactics, and artificial intelligence now increasingly offers new and worrying capabilities to them; creating and disseminating propaganda or developing attack methodologies, either by way of cyber attacks or in the ‘real-world’. To combat these complex and emerging threats, state agencies such as Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK must also embrace the opportunities of AI to be able to meet the threats head on, indeed get ahead of them, to mitigate risks, prevent escalation, and protect the public. In a climate of suspicion in some areas, the police use of AI in this domain must be managed and introduced in a fashion that fosters public trust and confidence. Accountability must be at its core.

items.title: AI-Based Financial Literacy, Perceived Ease of Use, Technology Readiness, and Personal Financial Management Behavior: the Mediating Role of Trust in AI
items.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed personal financial management, yet the gap between the adoption of digital financial tools and the financial literacy and trust required for effective use remains underexplored, particularly in urban Indonesia. This study examines the effects of AI-Based Financial Literacy, Perceived Ease of Use, and Technology Readiness on Personal Financial Management Behavior, with Trust in AI as a mediating variable. The study extends the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Technology Readiness Index (TRI) through the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework by integrating trust into an AI-based financial behavior model. A quantitative explanatory design was employed using survey data from 200 purposively selected respondents in Depok City, aged 18–40 years and using AI-based financial applications. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The results show that AI-Based Financial Literacy (β = 0.214; p = 0.001), Perceived Ease of Use (β = 0.187; p = 0.005), and Technology Readiness (β = 0.168; p = 0.008) positively and significantly affect Personal Financial Management Behavior. All hypotheses (H1–H6) were supported, with R² = 0.612. The findings confirm that Trust in AI mediates these relationships. The study contributes to TAM and TRI by highlighting trust as a mechanism linking AI-related capabilities to financial behavior and offers implications for developing an inclusive and trustworthy digital financial ecosystem.

items.title: AI-Based Inventory Management and Operational Efficiency
items.abstract: Abstract The increasing complexity and dynamism of global supply chains have rendered traditional inventory management approaches insufficient for meeting contemporary operational demands. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers transformative capabilities for inventory optimization through enhanced demand forecasting, automated replenishment, cost reduction, and supply chain resilience. This paper examines the integration of AI technologies in inventory management and their impact on operational efficiency through a systematic literature review and analysis of real-world case studies. The findings reveal that machine learning and deep learning models substantially outperform traditional statistical methods in demand prediction accuracy, particularly for intermittent and volatile demand patterns. AI-driven automated replenishment systems reduce stockouts and excess inventory, while predictive analytics enable proactive risk mitigation. Case analyses of Amazon, Walmart, and Zara demonstrate that organizations leveraging AI achieve measurable improvements in inventory turnover, waste reduction, and supply chain responsiveness. The paper concludes with a discussion of implementation challenges and future research directions, including the potential of generative AI and digital twin technologies.

items.title: AI-Enabled automated feedback and debriefing in simulation-based healthcare education: a systematic review of educational effectiveness
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into healthcare simulation to deliver individualized feedback and support reflective learning. Educational evaluations include procedural coaching, virtual patient encounters, and facilitator development. This review examined educational effectiveness while distinguishing observed performance from perceived competence and feedback feasibility. Original research published to May 2026 evaluating artificial intelligence enabled feedback or debriefing in healthcare simulation was reviewed. Comparative educational studies and complementary feedback validation or feasibility investigations were synthesized narratively. Outcomes included technical performance, clinical reasoning, communication, perceived competence, cognitive workload, and debriefing utility. Ten original reports comprised seven randomized trials and three prospective, pilot, or qualitative investigations. Surgical trials show improvements in selected performance measures, with benefits dependent on feedback timing, instructional design, and human participation. Personalized expert instruction informed by artificial intelligence exceeded artificial intelligence tutoring alone in practice and transfer tasks. Virtual patient feedback improved clinical reasoning in a small trial, while nursing simulations demonstrated gains in communication and perceived competence. Artificial intelligence enabled feedback offers benefits for simulation outcomes. Data for autonomous team debriefing is less developed than data for individualized coaching. Integration with educators, independent assessment, and longitudinal evaluation provides the strongest direction for educational implementation.

items.title: AI-Enabled Workforce Competency Mapping in Public Transport
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming modern Human Resource Management (HRM) by automating administrative procedures and providing data-driven insights into employee capabilities. Within public transport systems—where operational decisions span fleets, depots, customer interfaces, and administrative units—aligning workforce competencies with dynamic technological demands is essential. This study presents a quantitative framework that combines multiple linear regression and machine learning algorithms to map workforce competency preparedness and optimize training resource allocation. Using empirical data collected from operational, technical, supervisory, and customer-facing staff (N=397) across the Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation (APSRTC), we evaluate six core competency drivers: AI readiness, digital literacy, operational analytics competence, safety and compliance competence, learning agility, and institutional support. Multiple regression results indicate that all six drivers significantly influence competency preparedness (), with operational analytics competence () and safety and compliance competence () exerting the strongest standardized effects. Furthermore, comparative machine learning classification demonstrates that Logistic Regression (, Accuracy ) and Naïve Bayes () effectively categorize employees into low, moderate, and high training priority levels without circular prediction error. The study provides human resource practitioners and mobility policy-makers with an empirical, non-punitive decision support model for target-oriented workforce development.
